newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Data pause lets bears take over.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Data pause lets bears take over.

text.p: Sentiment in the U.S. fixed income market appears generally bearish and could continue to sour Wednesday amid a drought of economic data, analysts said.
Tuesday, Treasuries gave back their modest gains from the previous session, and analysts projected range-bound trade as players await key reports on price data and retail sales.
"There's not much to move the market, and I think it's just going to continue trading in a range close to where we are now," said James Blumenthal, an economist at MCM MoneyWatch Inc.
Even with no news to drive trading, many analysts said the market will probe negative territory, fearing upcoming data could be quite robust.
The March Producer Price Index (PPI) and retail sales releases are set for Friday, and the March Consumer Price Index (CPI) rolls out next Monday.

"The market is in a bearish mood already, and it doesn't take anything to set it off to the downside," said John Canavan, Treasury market analyst at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc. "I don't think there's anything to prop up the market in a sustainable way for the near term."
Expectations of future interest rate hikes and acute sensitivity to any inflation signals cloud the market's outlook, experts said.

Last Friday's employment report, for example, showed average hourly earnings grew 4.0 percent year-on-year, their fastest pace in about seven years. And statements from various regional Federal Reserve banks have repeated the mantra that economic growth remains strong.
"Market psychology remains pretty poor," Canavan said. "In general, people are waiting for more Fed rate hikes and are not seeing the economy slow down at the moment."
Trading Wednesday should hold within broad technical barriers, chartists said.
"We're going to be more range-bound between 106 and 108 in (June) bond futures," said Michael Krauss, managing director and chief technical strategist at Chase Securities Inc.
Looking to the cash bond, Krauss said selling would follow any dip in the 30-year yield to between 7.0 and 7.05 percent. The next key support level would be 7.24 percent, he said.
"I wouldn't want to stretch the envelope too much in terms of a bearish view, but I think the bears are still pretty much in control of the market," Krauss said.
The only scheduled news item potentially of interest to the market appears to be Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis president Gary Stern's speech at Moorhead State University in Moorhead, Minnesota.
The address is set for 1300 EDT/1700 GMT, and analysts expect it will retrace the lines of a speech Stern has given at several events in recent months.
"That's not going to do much," said MCM's Blumenthal.
